children: TOKYO--The Bank of Japan should act swiftly if price pressures mount and not delay interest-rate hikes, a hawkish policy board member said Thursday.

Speaking to business leaders in central Japan's Yamanashi prefecture, Naoki Tamura said the central bank needs to bring the policy rate to a neutral level soon, as financial conditions remain accommodative. A neutral rate is one that neither stimulates nor cools economic growth.
"While it is necessary to make these assessments 'thoroughly,' that does not mean 'slowly,'" he said. "In my view, the bank is currently expected to 'make haste slowly.'"
Tamura said it is possible to properly assess financial conditions within a few months of each rate hike, a comment that suggests the BOJ could tighten monetary policy again in the near term.
His remarks are likely to reinforce market expectations for another interest-rate increase next month.

Bets on a BOJ hike at its final meeting of the year have been building since the central bank declared last month that underlying inflation had reached its 2% target. Expectations of tightening by the Federal Reserve strengthen the argument for the BOJ to keep the rate gap with the U.S. from widening and weighing on an already weak yen.

One of the strongest proponents of higher interest rates on the nine-member board, Tamura didn't dissent when the BOJ opted to hold rates steady in October after raising the policy rate to 1.25% in September. But he has repeatedly warned of upside risks to prices and argued that the central bank needs to continue raising borrowing costs toward a neutral level.

Recent data have added to the case for further tightening. Government figures released last week showed that core consumer prices excluding fresh food rose 2.2% in October from a year earlier, picking up from September's 2.1% gain as energy prices rebounded.

"Given that underlying [consumer-price] inflation in Japan is less firmly anchored at the 2% target, I believe the bank is required to respond swiftly to signs of an upward deviation in prices, including by accelerating the pace of policy interest rate hikes," Tamura said.
